analysis.one_liner: Extends postpartum Medicaid coverage to a full year and funds programs to prevent maternal deaths, paid for partly by higher tobacco taxes.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced with 16 cosponsors, was referred to the Senate Finance Committee and never received a vote before the Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: The MOMMA's Act would extend Medicaid and CHIP coverage for new mothers from 60 days after childbirth to a full year, including dental care, with the federal government picking up the full cost of the extension at first. It would fund federal data collection on maternal deaths, grants to help states and hospitals adopt proven safety protocols, and training centers on implicit bias in maternity care. It would roughly double federal cigarette taxes and raise taxes on all other tobacco products to match.
analysis.who_benefits: Low-income pregnant and postpartum women who lose Medicaid coverage just weeks after giving birth would keep it for a year, including dental benefits; women at risk of preventable maternal deaths would benefit from standardized hospital safety protocols and better national death data; states and hospitals would get grants and technical support. Black women, who die from pregnancy-related causes at 3 to 4 times the rate of white women, are the group the bill most directly targets.

how_it_helps.text: Extends Medicaid and CHIP coverage for pregnant and postpartum women from 60 days after the pregnancy to a full year, with the federal government paying 100% of the cost of the extension for the first five years [S2] [S3].
Requires Medicaid and CHIP to cover dental services for pregnant and postpartum women, since oral health is tied to birth outcomes [S2] [S3].

Directs the CDC to standardize state reporting of maternal deaths and issue best practices, because the U.S. has had no official maternal mortality rate since 2007 due to unstandardized state data [S2] [S3].

Creates grant programs to spread hospital 'maternal safety bundles' — standardized checklists for hemorrhage, hypertension, and other leading causes of maternal death — which helped California cut its maternal mortality rate to levels comparable to the United Kingdom's [S2] [S3].

Establishes regional centers to train health professionals on implicit bias and cultural competency, addressing the finding that Black women die of pregnancy-related causes at 3 to 4 times the rate of white women [S2] [S3].
Raises cigarette taxes from $50.33 to $100.66 per thousand and equalizes taxes across all tobacco products, with revenues not earmarked to the maternal health programs [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Smokers and other tobacco users would pay roughly twice the current federal cigarette tax, a cost that falls hardest on lower-income smokers; taxpayers generally fund the new grant programs and the extended Medicaid coverage, and states must maintain their current pregnancy-related Medicaid eligibility for five years.

drawbacks.text: The cigarette tax increase is regressive: it roughly doubles the federal excise tax on every pack, and its burden falls disproportionately on lower-income smokers, the same income group the bill's Medicaid extension serves [S3].
The bill authorizes new annual appropriations for grants, data systems, and training centers for five or more years, adding federal spending without a dedicated funding source [S3].

It would impose a one-time 'floor stocks' tax on retailers and distributors holding untaxed tobacco inventory when the higher rates take effect, plus a five-year prohibition on states tightening pregnancy-related Medicaid eligibility [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core provisions respond to a well-documented crisis — more than 60% of maternal deaths are estimated preventable, and nearly half occur after the 60-day Medicaid window closes. The main cost is a steeply regressive tobacco tax, which discourages smoking but is not linked to funding the programs, and modest new federal spending. On balance the benefits to new mothers outweigh the costs, though a fair reading notes the tax hits the poor and the revenue is unallocated.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, which never acted on it, and it died when the Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Sen. Durbin introduced the MOMMA's Act on March 27, 2019, with eight original cosponsors including one independent [S3].
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Finance the same day; no further action was ever recorded [S5].
The bill finished with 16 cosponsors, 14 Democrats and 2 independents, and never received a committee markup, floor vote, or House action before the 116th Congress ended [S4] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The Senate Finance Committee's inaction preserved the status quo, which was better for tobacco companies facing a doubled cigarette tax and for members unwilling to take a vote on new health spending; new mothers lost the chance at a year of postpartum coverage. (Notably, Congress later enacted a version of the 12-month postpartum Medicaid extension through a different bill, the American Rescue Plan, in 2021.)

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Tobacco companies and the committee that never acted

for.name: Sen. Richard Durbin
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and led its introduction.

for.name: 16 Senate cosponsors
for.what_they_did: 14 Democrats and 2 independents signed on as cosponsors; no Republican did.

against.name: Senate Committee on Finance
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Sen. Chuck Grassley (R-IA)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on March 27, 2019 and never scheduled a markup or reported it out; the bill's entire Senate action history is the referral.

against.name: Senate Republican leadership
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the Senate floor; no bill referred to committee and not reported can reach a vote without the majority scheduling it.

sides.party_line_note: All 16 cosponsors were Democrats or independents, including independent Sen. Angus King; no Republican sponsored or cosponsored, and the bill died in committee under Republican majority control with no vote ever taken.

industries.note: The bill doubles the federal cigarette excise tax and raises every other tobacco product's tax to match, a direct hit to industry revenue and a large cost to smokers. The industry's interest in keeping taxes low runs against the bill's public-health purpose of discouraging smoking.

The bill funds hospital participation in maternal safety collaboratives and standardizes emergency obstetric protocols. Providers gain resources while patients gain safer care, though providers also absorb protocol changes.
Extending postpartum Medicaid coverage from 60 days to a year, federally funded at 100% initially, means additional covered months and revenue for insurers serving Medicaid patients.
Requiring Medicaid and CHIP to cover dental care for pregnant and postpartum women opens a new covered patient population for dental providers, while low-income mothers gain access to care.

industries.industry: Medical schools and health professional training programs
industries.note: The bill authorizes $5 million a year for regional centers of excellence on implicit bias and cultural competency, channeling new federal funds to teaching institutions focused on maternal health.
